lessons.title: Why screening starts with CC and MLO
lessons.summary: The two standard projections are the accreditation pair and the everyday tissue-coverage baseline.

explanation.heading: Two views, complementary tissue
explanation.body: A typical screening mammogram uses two projections of each breast: **craniocaudal (CC)** and **mediolateral oblique (MLO)**. The goal of positioning is not a pretty outline — it is to project **as much breast tissue as possible** onto the detector so disease is less likely to be missed because tissue was left off the image.

explanation.heading: Why accreditation cares about this pair
explanation.body: Under MQSA, when an accreditation body reviews clinical images for each unit, the facility submits **CC and MLO views from two examinations**. FDA’s EQUIP FAQ also notes that those same standard CC/MLO views — even when acquired during a diagnostic exam — can be scored on the eight clinical image attributes.

explanation.heading: What “good positioning” means in the regulation
explanation.body: Among those eight attributes, **positioning** means imaging enough breast tissue that cancers are not likely to be missed because of inadequate positioning. Detailed score-sheet criteria live in accreditation materials (link-only); this module teaches the public and openly restatable evaluation ideas without inventing correction recipes.

lessons.example: A facility preparing accreditation clinical images pulls a fatty-breast exam and a dense-breast exam and submits the CC and MLO pairs for each unit — the same views technologists produce every day.

misconception.belief: If the nipple looks centered, positioning is automatically acceptable.
misconception.correction: Centering alone is not the regulatory goal. The positioning attribute asks whether enough tissue was imaged; accreditation materials add specific landmarks such as posterior tissue depth.

variants.simpler: CC + MLO are the everyday pair and the accreditation pair. Positioning succeeds when enough tissue is on the image.
variants.example: If only a pretty nipple profile is achieved but posterior tissue is missing, the positioning attribute can still fail.
variants.deeper: ARRT names the ACR 1999 Clinical Image Quality manual as a positioning reference; Mammo does not reproduce that copyrighted book. Use ACR accreditation links alongside the open sources cited here.

lessons.observationPrompt: Ask your preceptor which landmarks your facility checklist uses for CC and MLO acceptance — then compare that list to the MQSA positioning attribute wording.

lessons.title: CC view: purpose and evaluation ideas
lessons.summary: CC images the breast from superior to inferior and is judged by posterior tissue coverage relative to the MLO.

explanation.heading: Purpose
explanation.body: The **craniocaudal (CC)** projection images the breast along a superior-to-inferior beam path. Together with the MLO, it helps show tissue that one oblique view alone may under-represent — especially more medial tissue that is harder to include on MLO.

explanation.heading: Evaluation ideas you can source
explanation.body: An open ACR–AAPM–SIIM digital mammography image-quality guideline (link-only) describes clinical positioning assessment using the **posterior nipple line (PNL)**: on the CC, the distance from nipple to the posterior edge of the image should be **no more than about 1 cm less** than the MLO PNL (nipple to the anterior edge of pectoralis). That comparison is about **retromammary / posterior tissue**, not a cosmetic nipple placement contest.

explanation.heading: What this lesson does not invent
explanation.body: Facility score sheets may add more CC checks (skin folds, exaggeration, nipple profile rules). Those details belong in ACR accreditation materials and clinical preceptorship. This lesson stays with sourced purpose and the PNL comparison idea.

lessons.example: You compare the CC and MLO of the same breast: if the CC PNL is more than about a centimeter shorter than the MLO PNL, posterior tissue may be under-represented on the CC.

misconception.belief: Seeing pectoralis on every CC is required.
misconception.correction: The open guideline discussion focuses on posterior tissue depth via PNL comparison; pectoralis visibility on CC is not framed there as a universal requirement.

variants.simpler: CC is top-to-bottom. Check that posterior tissue depth is close to the MLO using the PNL idea.
variants.example: A CC that looks neat but is much shorter front-to-back than the MLO may have left posterior tissue off the detector.

lessons.title: MLO view: purpose and evaluation ideas
lessons.summary: MLO follows the pectoralis orientation to include posterior and axillary-tail tissue and is checked for muscle shape and depth.

explanation.heading: Purpose
explanation.body: The **mediolateral oblique (MLO)** is angled to travel roughly along the pectoralis major. That geometry is how technologists bring **posterior breast tissue** and the **axillary tail** onto the image — tissue that a true lateral or a CC alone may not show as well.

explanation.heading: Sourced evaluation ideas
explanation.body: The same open ACR–AAPM–SIIM guideline (link-only) states that on MLO the **anterior edge of pectoralis should be convex**, and it is **desirable for the muscle to extend to the level of the nipple**. The MLO PNL is drawn **perpendicular to the muscle**, often near **45°**.

explanation.heading: Inframammary fold and other checklist items
explanation.body: Many facility and accreditation checklists also look for an open inframammary fold and freedom from large obscuring folds. Treat those as clinical/accreditation criteria to learn with your preceptor and ACR materials — this module does not invent numeric pass/fail rules beyond what the cited open sources support.

lessons.example: On a schematic MLO, a wide superior pectoralis band that narrows and reaches near nipple level with a convex anterior edge matches the sourced “desirable” muscle description.

misconception.belief: A steeper angle is always better.
misconception.correction: Angle serves tissue coverage along the pectoralis. The sourced evaluation language focuses on muscle contour and depth relative to the nipple/PNL, not on maximizing degrees for their own sake.

variants.simpler: MLO follows the muscle to catch posterior and axillary-tail tissue. Look for a convex pectoralis that ideally reaches nipple level.
variants.example: If the muscle stops high above the nipple and posterior tissue looks truncated, discuss the image with your preceptor before assuming it is acceptable.

lessons.title: Posterior nipple line: comparing CC and MLO depth
lessons.summary: PNL is a simple length comparison that asks whether the CC captured nearly as much posterior depth as the MLO.

explanation.heading: What PNL measures
explanation.body: Think of PNL as a **depth ruler**. On MLO it runs from the nipple perpendicular to the anterior pectoralis edge. On CC it runs from the nipple back to the posterior image edge (chest-wall side of the image).

explanation.heading: The approximate comparison
explanation.body: Sourced teaching (link-only guideline): the CC PNL should be **no more than about 1 cm less** than the MLO PNL. A large gap suggests the CC may not include as much posterior tissue as the MLO demonstrated was available.

explanation.heading: Beta caution
explanation.body: Exact facility tolerances, measurement technique on DBT slices, and how to correct a short CC are clinical skills. This app stays at the comparison concept and keeps related quiz items out of any clinically reviewed pool.

lessons.example: MLO PNL measures about 11 cm; CC PNL measures about 9.5 cm — within about 1 cm — so posterior depth roughly matches. If CC were 8 cm, you would flag posterior tissue for review.

misconception.belief: PNL is a pathology measurement of a lesion.
misconception.correction: Here PNL is a positioning geometry check comparing how far back tissue is included on CC versus MLO.

variants.simpler: PNL asks: did the CC go nearly as far back as the MLO?
variants.example: Draw both lengths on a schematic (not a real mammogram) and compare; a big CC shortfall means missing posterior tissue.

lessons.title: Why we compress (purpose, not paddle QC)
lessons.summary: Compression exists to separate tissue, reduce motion, and improve the radiograph — explain that in plain language.

explanation.heading: Patient-friendly purpose
explanation.body: NCI tells patients the breast is pressed between two plates because **pressing helps get a better x-ray picture**. Several images are taken from different angles with repositioning between exposures.

explanation.heading: What reviewers mean by the compression attribute
explanation.body: In MQSA clinical image review, **compression** means it was applied so overlying tissue is less likely to obscure findings and so **motion artifact** is minimized.

explanation.heading: Image-quality reasons (link-only detail)
explanation.body: An open professional guideline restates additional mechanisms: immobilization and shorter exposure (less blur), thinner more uniform tissue (less scatter and superposition), and lower breast dose. This lesson is about **why** we compress — not about performing manufacturer compression-force QC tests.

lessons.example: A patient asks why it has to hurt. You explain that firm, even compression spreads tissue so small findings are less hidden and so the exposure can be shorter, which also reduces blur from motion.

misconception.belief: Compression is mainly to reduce dose, so lighter compression is fine if dose looks acceptable.
misconception.correction: Dose reduction is one benefit discussed in professional guidance, but the clinical-image attribute emphasizes reducing obscuration and motion. Inadequate compression can fail image quality even when dose is not the complaint.

variants.simpler: Compression separates overlapping tissue and reduces motion so the picture is clearer.
variants.example: If a patient moves because compression was released too early, motion blur can hide calcifications even when positioning landmarks look present.

lessons.observationPrompt: Listen to how your preceptor explains compression in one sentence. Practice a version that is honest about discomfort without over-promising painlessness.

lessons.title: View and laterality labels near the axilla
lessons.summary: Every image carries permanent identifiers; view/laterality belong near the axilla and must not hide anatomy.

explanation.heading: Required identification
explanation.body: MQSA requires each mammographic image to show, permanently and legibly, identifiers including patient name plus an additional identifier, date of examination, **view and laterality**, facility name/location, technologist identification, cassette/screen identification (as applicable), and unit identification when a facility has more than one unit.

explanation.heading: Where view/laterality go
explanation.body: View and laterality must be placed **near the axilla**. No label may obscure anatomic structures.

explanation.heading: Why technologists care during positioning
explanation.body: Label location is part of examination identification — one of the eight clinical image attributes. A perfectly positioned breast with missing or misplaced markers still fails identification.

lessons.example: On a right MLO schematic, the RMLO marker sits in the axillary region, not over the nipple or mid-breast parenchyma.

misconception.belief: Digital systems auto-tag views, so on-image markers no longer matter.
misconception.correction: MQSA still requires the view and laterality information on the image near the axilla in a permanent, unambiguous form. Know your facility’s compliant labeling workflow.

variants.simpler: Put view + side near the axilla. Never cover anatomy.
variants.example: If a marker lands over dense tissue, correct labeling before the image is accepted for interpretation.

history.note: AI-assisted draft source-checked against cited public MQSA/NCI evidence.

lessons.title: Screening versus diagnostic: views and purpose
lessons.summary: Screening uses routine views in asymptomatic patients; diagnostic exams are individualized and often add angles.

explanation.heading: NCI’s plain distinction
explanation.body: Screening mammograms look for cancer **before symptoms**. Diagnostic mammograms evaluate a **lump or other change**. Same machines; diagnostic work usually needs **images from more angles**, which means a higher radiation dose than a routine screen.

explanation.heading: MQSA audit wording
explanation.body: For medical outcomes audit definitions, a **screening** mammogram is routine views of an asymptomatic patient; a **diagnostic** mammogram is an individualized examination for clinical findings or an abnormal screening result.

explanation.heading: Positioning implication
explanation.body: Diagnostic work may still include standard CC/MLO plus problem-solving views. EQUIP guidance notes that standard CC/MLO acquired in a diagnostic exam can still be reviewed on the eight attributes.

lessons.example: An asymptomatic patient gets routine bilateral CC and MLO. A patient recalled for a new asymmetry may return for additional angled or spot views tailored to that finding.

misconception.belief: Diagnostic always means a completely different machine.
misconception.correction: NCI states the same machines are used; the difference is the individualized imaging approach and typically more angles.

variants.simpler: Screening = routine views, no symptoms. Diagnostic = tailored views for a problem.
variants.example: A callback for calcifications may add magnification views even though the screening CC/MLO already exist.

history.note: AI-assisted draft source-checked against cited public MQSA/NCI evidence.

lessons.title: Ask about implants before you image
lessons.summary: MQSA requires an implant inquiry and views that maximize visible tissue unless a physician modifies the plan.

explanation.heading: The required question
explanation.body: Each facility must have a procedure to **ask whether the patient has breast implants before** the mammographic exam.

explanation.heading: The imaging expectation
explanation.body: Unless **contraindicated** or **modified by a physician’s directions**, patients with implants must have mammographic views that **maximize visualization of breast tissue**.

explanation.heading: Why the question comes first
explanation.body: NCI notes implants can hide tissue and that patients should tell the facility. Knowing implant status before positioning prevents a standard four-view habit from being applied blindly when a modified approach is needed.

lessons.example: During history intake you ask about implants and reconstruction. The patient reports bilateral augmentation; you follow the facility implant procedure rather than assuming a non-implant screening set.

misconception.belief: If the order does not mention implants, you do not need to ask.
misconception.correction: MQSA puts the inquiry procedure on the facility — ask before the exam, not only when the requisition happens to mention implants.

variants.simpler: Ask first. Then maximize visible tissue unless a physician changes the plan.
variants.example: A patient with a history of implant exchange still needs the inquiry — status can change between exams.

history.note: AI-assisted draft source-checked against cited public MQSA/NCI evidence.

lessons.title: Implant-displaced views: what they are for
lessons.summary: Displacement views pull native tissue forward so it can be imaged with less implant overlap — still under MQSA’s maximize-tissue rule.

explanation.heading: The problem implants create
explanation.body: NCI states implants can **hide some breast tissue**, making unusual changes harder to see. Patients with implants should continue mammography (with the usual reconstruction exception after mastectomy) and tell the facility.

explanation.heading: Displacement views
explanation.body: NCI names **implant displacement views** as a special technique that may be used. In plain terms, native breast tissue is drawn anteriorly while the implant is displaced back, so compressed tissue can be imaged with less implant in the field.

explanation.heading: Regulatory frame — not a step-by-step recipe
explanation.body: MQSA requires views that maximize tissue visualization unless contraindicated or physician-modified. Exact hand positions, when displacement is impossible (for example encapsulation), and how many views your facility acquires are clinical protocol details for preceptorship and link-only professional materials — not invented here.

lessons.example: After implant-status confirmation, the technologist acquires the facility’s implant protocol, which includes displacement views intended to show more native tissue than implant-in-field images alone.

misconception.belief: Implant displacement replaces the need to maximize tissue overall.
misconception.correction: Displacement is a technique in service of MQSA’s maximize-visualization expectation (unless modified). It is not a loophole to skip tissue that still needs imaging.

variants.simpler: Displacement moves tissue forward so the implant hides less of it.
variants.example: If displacement is not possible, follow physician direction / facility procedure — do not invent a workaround from memory of a textbook diagram.

lessons.title: Problem-solving views: spot and magnification purposes
lessons.summary: Diagnostic work adds tailored views; magnification is an equipment-capable tool for detail, not a screening default.

explanation.heading: Why extra views exist
explanation.body: When screening is abnormal or the patient has symptoms, imaging becomes individualized. Additional projections and compression techniques are chosen to answer a specific question — not to repeat the screening set for its own sake.

explanation.heading: Magnification capability (equipment fact)
explanation.body: MQSA requires that systems used for noninterventional problem solving have **magnification** capability, provide at least one magnification value in the **1.4–2.0** range, and be able to operate with the **grid removed**. Those are equipment design facts that support magnified detail imaging.

explanation.heading: Spot compression — purpose level
explanation.body: Spot compression uses a smaller paddle to compress a limited area more effectively, helping separate superimposed tissue. Specific correction sequences for every finding type need clinical teaching materials; this lesson stays at purpose.

lessons.example: A cluster of calcifications on screening CC/MLO is recalled for magnification views on a system that can magnify in the required range with the grid out.

misconception.belief: Any zoom on a workstation replaces a true magnification acquisition.
misconception.correction: Workstation zoom enlarges pixels already acquired. Geometric magnification (with the equipment capability MQSA describes) changes acquisition geometry for finer detail.

variants.simpler: Problem-solving views answer a question. Magnification is an acquisition technique with MQSA equipment requirements.
variants.example: Spot compression presses a small area to untangle overlapping densities.

lessons.title: Additional views: laterals and tissue not on the standard pair
lessons.summary: ML/LM and other extras exist to problem-solve; keep the side of interest close to the receptor — details stay in clinical teaching.

explanation.heading: When the standard pair is not enough
explanation.body: Diagnostic problem-solving may add **true lateral** views (mediolateral ML or lateromedial LM), exaggerated CC views for axillary/lateral tissue, cleavage views for far-medial tissue, rolled views to separate superimposed densities, or tangential views for skin findings. Names in the ARRT procedures domain are vocabulary you must recognize.

explanation.heading: A durable geometry idea
explanation.body: For lateral imaging, put the **side of interest closer to the image receptor** to reduce geometric blur and magnification of the region being evaluated. That principle is general radiographic geometry applied to breast laterals.

explanation.heading: Source honesty
explanation.body: Step-by-step positioning corrections for each extra view are not invented here. Use preceptorship plus link-only ACR/ARRT references. Quiz items in this lesson stay at purpose and selection, with qualified-review flags.

lessons.example: A lateral lesion seen on MLO is clearer on an ML with the lateral breast against the receptor than on an LM that puts that tissue farther from the detector.

misconception.belief: XCCL is just a badly positioned CC.
misconception.correction: Exaggerated CC is an intentional additional view to include tissue that the standard CC did not demonstrate — not an accidental failure of a screening CC.

variants.simpler: Extra views are tools for specific tissue or findings. Laterals: region of interest toward the receptor.
variants.example: If medial tissue is missing on both CCs, a cleavage view is a purposeful add-on, not a repeat of the same CC.

lessons.title: Special circumstances: adapt, document, do not invent rules
lessons.summary: Body habitus, surgery, mobility limits, and lactation change what is achievable — maximize tissue and document limits.

explanation.heading: Same goal, different path
explanation.body: MQSA’s positioning attribute still asks whether **enough tissue** was imaged. Patients with kyphosis, limited arm mobility, very large or very small breasts, post-surgical contour change, or lactation may need adapted setups. Adaptation is not optional courtesy — it is how you pursue the same tissue-coverage goal.

explanation.heading: What we will not fabricate
explanation.body: There is no open federal table that lists a single correct mosaic tiling pattern or a universal wheelchair sequence. Those procedures come from clinical training and facility protocol. This lesson teaches the decision frame: maximize tissue, communicate, document limitations, and escalate when a physician-modified approach is needed.

explanation.heading: Implants and reconstruction reminder
explanation.body: Implant inquiry remains mandatory. NCI notes that most patients with post-mastectomy implant reconstruction usually do not need mammography of the reconstructed breast — a different pathway than augmentation with native tissue present.

lessons.example: A patient cannot elevate the arm for a classic MLO. You adapt with your preceptor’s method, obtain the best achievable tissue, and document the limitation rather than forcing a textbook pose that leaves tissue off the image.

misconception.belief: If the patient cannot do the textbook pose, the exam cannot meet MQSA.
misconception.correction: The standard is adequate tissue imaging and compliant practice — not identical body posture for every patient. Document limits and follow physician/facility direction when the approach must change.

variants.simpler: Adapt to the patient; keep the tissue-coverage goal; document what you could not show.
variants.example: Post-mastectomy reconstruction with implant often means no mammogram of that side — confirm history rather than assuming augmentation technique.

lessons.observationPrompt: With supervision, watch one adapted exam (mobility limit, large breast, or postsurgical). Note what was documented when a landmark could not be shown.

lessons.title: Checking a CC: nipple, posterior depth, and edges
lessons.summary: A well-positioned CC shows the nipple in profile near midline, retroglandular fat at the back of the image, no medial or lateral cut-off, and a PNL close to the MLO's.

explanation.heading: Beam path
explanation.body: The **craniocaudal (CC)** beam travels straight down from above the breast. Together with the MLO it forms the four-view screening set that ACR also uses for accreditation clinical-image review.

explanation.heading: Nipple
explanation.body: Aim for the nipple **in profile** and **near midline**. One 2022 open-access study describes acceptable deviation as no more than about **20°** medially or laterally. Pulling the nipple far off midline (excessive exaggeration) can drop **medial or lateral posterior tissue** off the image. ACR's quality-improvement table requires the nipple in profile on **at least one view of each breast**.

explanation.heading: Posterior depth
explanation.body: Look for **retroglandular fat**, the dark band nearest the chest wall. The pectoralis shows on the CC in only about **30%** of women, so missing muscle alone is not a failure. Then compare depth with the MLO using the **posterior nipple line (PNL)**: the CC PNL should be **within about 1 cm** of the MLO PNL.

explanation.heading: Everything else
explanation.body: Check that no medial or lateral tissue is **cut off**, there is **no motion**, **skin folds** do not hide tissue, and nothing else (chin, shoulder, hand, the other breast) lies over the breast.

lessons.example: MLO PNL is 10.5 cm and CC PNL is 9.0 cm. The CC is 1.5 cm short, more than the 1 cm tolerance, so posterior tissue may be missing from the CC.

misconception.belief: Every acceptable CC shows the pectoralis muscle.
misconception.correction: ACR's positioning table notes the muscle appears on the CC in only about 30% of women. Judge posterior depth with retroglandular fat and the PNL comparison.

variants.simpler: CC check: nipple in profile and centered, dark fat band at the back, no tissue cut off at either side, PNL within 1 cm of the MLO.
variants.example: A neat-looking CC with the nipple pulled well to one side and lateral posterior tissue missing fails on exaggeration, even though it looks tidy.
variants.deeper: These criteria come from ACR's quality-improvement positioning table (ACR says it is not accreditation scoring), the ACR–AAPM–SIIM image-quality guideline, and a CC BY 2022 study. ACR accreditation reviewers use the Clinical Image Evaluation section of the 1999 ACR QC manual, which Mammo has not accessed. Needs confirmation by a qualified reviewer.

lessons.observationPrompt: On your next screening exam (with your preceptor), find the retroglandular fat on each CC and measure both PNLs. Is the CC within 1 cm of the MLO?

lessons.title: Checking an MLO: pectoralis, PNL, and the inframammary fold
lessons.summary: A well-positioned MLO shows a relaxed pectoralis that is wide at the top, convex or straight, and reaches the PNL or lower, plus an open inframammary fold, the nipple in profile, and posterior tissue.

explanation.heading: Why the MLO matters
explanation.body: The **mediolateral oblique (MLO)** follows the line of the pectoralis. It shows the **upper outer quadrant** with more breast tissue than any other single view.

explanation.heading: Pectoralis
explanation.body: Good muscle is **wide at the top and narrows going down**, with an anterior edge that is **convex or straight**. Its lower edge should reach the **PNL (about nipple level) or below**. In ACR's quality-improvement table, muscle ending **within 1 cm** of the PNL only partially meets the criterion; **more than 1 cm short**, a thin sliver, or a **concave** front edge is inadequate.

explanation.heading: PNL on the MLO
explanation.body: Draw the PNL from the nipple **perpendicular to the front edge of the pectoralis** (often about 45° on the image). Use this length as the reference for the CC comparison.

explanation.heading: Lower breast and placement
explanation.body: The **inframammary fold (IMF)** should be **open without folds**. The breast should be **lifted, not sagging**, and **centered** on the detector. If it sits too high, the image shows too much abdomen and not enough axilla. Also check for the nipple in profile, retroglandular fat, no skin folds, and no motion.

lessons.example: The MLO pectoralis ends 1.8 cm above the PNL and its front edge curves inward. Both findings point to inadequate muscle, so posterior tissue may be under-represented.

misconception.belief: If any pectoralis shows on the MLO, the view is acceptable.
misconception.correction: The muscle needs adequate width, a convex or straight front edge, and should reach the PNL. A thin, concave muscle that stops well above the PNL is inadequate.

variants.simpler: MLO check: muscle wide at the top, convex, down to nipple level; IMF open; breast lifted and centered.
variants.example: An MLO with lots of abdomen at the bottom and the axilla cut off has the breast placed too high on the detector.
variants.deeper: Criteria come from ACR's quality-improvement positioning table (not accreditation scoring), the ACR–AAPM–SIIM guideline, and a CC BY 2022 study. How to fix a short muscle or closed IMF is hands-on technique to learn from a preceptor. Needs confirmation by a qualified reviewer.

lessons.observationPrompt: With your preceptor, trace the pectoralis on several MLOs: is it convex, wide superiorly, and down to the PNL? Is the IMF open?

lessons.title: Post-surgical and special-anatomy imaging pathways
lessons.summary: Document surgical and implant history, maximize tissue under MQSA unless modified/contraindicated, and use NCI implant-displacement concepts when implants are present—without inventing reconstruction recipes.

explanation.heading: History first
explanation.body: Ask and document implants, reconstruction, reduction, lumpectomy/mastectomy, radiation, and lactation status before positioning. MQSA requires facilities to inquire about implants before the exam.

explanation.heading: Implants and displacement
explanation.body: NCI describes implant displacement (Eklund-style) views that pull breast tissue forward while the implant is displaced back, plus standard implant-included views when appropriate. MQSA expects the facility to maximize imaged tissue unless contraindicated or modified.

explanation.heading: Limits of this lesson
explanation.body: Detailed hand maneuvers for irradiated, male, or complex reconstruction anatomy are preceptorship/link-only skills. Your job in this beta lesson is safe history-taking, honest documentation, and knowing when to involve a supervising technologist or radiologist—not inventing mosaic rules.

lessons.example: Patient with subglandular implants: you document implant type/location if known, obtain implant-included and displacement views per protocol, and note any modification when tissue cannot be maximized.

misconception.correction: NCI and MQSA frame specialized implant imaging pathways; do not cancel screening solely because implants are present.

variants.simpler: Ask about surgery/implants. Maximize tissue unless modified. Use displacement views when protocol calls for them.
variants.example: Reconstruction without native tissue may change which views are possible—document and follow the order/protocol.

lessons.title: Breast ultrasound and MRI: roles beside mammography
lessons.summary: Ultrasound and MRI are adjunct tools with different physics. High-risk pathways may add MRI to mammography; dense-breast supplemental imaging remains an evidence-insufficient area for average-risk screening outcomes.

explanation.heading: Ultrasound
explanation.body: NCI: breast ultrasound uses sound waves. It may be offered in addition to mammography for dense breasts, but it is **not known** whether that supplemental screening improves health outcomes.

explanation.heading: MRI
explanation.body: NCI: breast MRI uses magnets and radio waves (**no ionizing radiation**) and is more sensitive than mammography alone for some high-risk patients. High-risk screening often pairs annual MRI with mammography (ACS high-risk pathway is link-only). Dense-breast supplemental MRI outcome benefit is similarly unproven in NCI/USPSTF framing.

explanation.heading: Technologist prep boundaries
explanation.body: Confirm the ordered modality, allergies/contrast instructions when the order requires them, and metal/implant screening per facility MRI safety—without inventing contrast doses. Mammography technologists coordinate schedules and explanations; they do not independently convert a mammogram order into MRI.

lessons.example: Patient with dense breasts asks for "the MRI instead." You: "MRI is a different test—sometimes added for high-risk plans. Supplemental imaging for density alone is not settled as an outcome benefit; your clinician decides whether ultrasound or MRI is ordered."

misconception.belief: Dense breasts automatically require screening MRI under USPSTF.
misconception.correction: USPSTF/NCI: evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against supplemental ultrasound/MRI solely for dense breasts after a negative screen.

variants.simpler: US = sound waves. MRI = magnets, no x-rays, more sensitive in many high-risk pathways. Density add-ons need clinician orders.
variants.example: Do not promise MRI mortality benefit for average-risk dense breasts.

lessons.title: Biopsy guidance, wires, specimens, and clips—terminology
lessons.summary: Know the sourced definitions: stereotactic and ultrasound-guided biopsy, wire localization, specimens, and biopsy clips. Detailed device steps stay in preceptorship.

explanation.heading: Image-guided biopsy types
explanation.body: NCI Dictionary: **stereotactic biopsy** uses a computer and 3D scanning to find a site and guide tissue removal. **Ultrasound-guided biopsy** uses ultrasound to find the abnormality and guide removal. Core vs fine-needle distinctions appear under needle biopsy definitions.

explanation.heading: Wire localization
explanation.body: Wire/needle localization marks a nonpalpable abnormality for surgery: imaging guides a hooked wire through a hollow needle; the needle comes out, the wire stays until the biopsy/surgery, then the wire is removed.

explanation.heading: Specimen and clip
explanation.body: A **biopsy specimen** is tissue removed for microscopy to look for disease. A **breast biopsy clip/marker** is a tiny metal marker left so the site can be seen on later mammograms or other imaging; NCI states it does not cause pain or harm.

lessons.example: After a stereotactic core biopsy, you obtain post-biopsy mammograms to document clip location per protocol and handle the specimen container labeled for pathology—without interpreting the histology yourself.

misconception.belief: A biopsy clip is a temporary suture that must be removed in a week.
misconception.correction: NCI: the clip/marker is left in the breast to mark the site on future imaging and does not harm the body.

variants.simpler: Stereo = x-ray/3D guided sampling. US-guided = sound-wave guided. Wires mark for surgery. Clips mark the site later.
variants.example: Specimen goes to pathology; clip stays for future localization on images.
